source: General Directorate of Agriculture (អគ្គនាយកដ្ឋានកសិកម្ម), Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Cambodia — 'ផលិតកម្មដំណំពោតផ្អែម' (Sweet Corn Production Handbook), produced under the Agriculture Development and Economic Growth Project in partnership with SNV (Netherlands Development Organisation); compiled by staff of the Rice Crop Department and the Extension Department of GDA
text:
Corn (ពោត) is a widely grown crop worldwide and a staple food for hundreds of millions of people. In Cambodia, farmers across most provinces grow corn mainly for food, eaten boiled, roasted/grilled, or steamed, as well as for animal feed. Corn was first introduced to Cambodia between the 17th and 18th centuries during the period of French colonization, and became recognized as a national crop from 1910 onward.

Corn kernels contain approximately 10.8% water, 10% protein, 4.3% fat, 73.4% carbohydrate, and 1.4% fiber, among other nutrients.

Uses of corn include: as a staple food for some countries that rely on corn as their main food source; as a supplementary food eaten boiled, roasted/grilled, or steamed, from the young (milk) stage through to maturity, and processed into corn rice, corn flour, corn cakes, and similar products; as an industrial raw material, where stalks and cobs are used for fuel or burning, red corn kernels are ground for animal feed, and waxy/glutinous corn kernels are ground into starch used for glue, cosmetics, soap, and metal casting products; corn is also processed to extract protein and starch for pharmaceutical use, and used to make bread, cooking oil, corn syrup, and corn wine. Corn is also valuable for scientific research, allowing scientists to study reproductive characteristics and varietal changes across generations of the species.

Sweet corn (ពោតផ្អែម) specifically originates from Central America. It is a variety with a larger stem diameter than other local varieties, with a stem height of about 180 cm and large, elongated ears; it is mostly eaten fresh/young. Sweet corn comes in three colors: yellow, white, and mixed (a mix of yellow and white kernels on the same ear). Sweet corn kernels are drier than other corn varieties and are more brittle and easy to peel. Sweet corn kernels contain 16-20% protein. Sweet corn is generally grown mainly for human food consumption.
